name: The three states and the fourth (waking, dream, deep sleep, turīya)

definitions.definition: In the Kārikā: viśva (waking-station, outward-knowing, enjoyer of the gross, right eye), taijasa (inward, enjoyer of the subtle, mind), prājña (mass of cognition, enjoyer of bliss, space of the heart) — one alone threefold; the fourth is not bound by cause or effect and has no seed-sleep, sleep or dream; it is reached when the two errors are exhausted.

In the Kārikā: ruler of the ending of all sorrows, non-dual, imperishable, all-pervading, all-seeing, without cause/effect bond, without seed-sleep. | In the Kārikā ch.3: unborn, sleepless, dreamless, nameless, formless, shining once for all, omniscient; free of speech and thought; motionless and fearless samādhi; self-abiding, peaceful, inexpressible. | In 4.81: unborn, sleepless, dreamless, dawning of itself, once-shone; in 4.80 the steady abiding of one who has turned back, the domain of the awakened; 4.100 the state hard to see, very deep, unborn, of sameness, without multiplicity.

name: The measures of Oṃ (a, u, m)

definitions.definition: In the Kārikā: a-viśva (first/obtaining), u-taijasa (exaltation/in-between), m-prājña (measuring/merging); the measureless Oṃ is the stilling of duality.
In the Kārikā: the praṇava is fearless brahman, both lower and higher, beginning-middle-end of all, the Lord in the heart.

In the Kārikā ch.1: the beginning-less sleep of the jīva; duality is mere māyā and non-duality is the ultimate. | In ch.2: the self's own māyā by which it imagines itself and the entities and by which it is deluded; the world is seen like dream, magic and the gandharva city. | In ch.4: the māyā elephant, the māyā seed and sprout, the jīva made of māyā; the birth of dharmas is like māyā and that māyā does not exist (4.58).

name: Vaitathya, the unreality of dream and waking entities

definitions.definition: The wise say the entities are unreal, shown from dream (inner place, short time, chariots absent), and waking is one with dream by the sameness of distinctions; both what is imagined within and grasped outside are unreal in each state; the self imagines all by its own māyā. | In 4.31–4.41 and 4.61–4.67 the argument of prakaraṇa 2 is resumed: dream and waking objects are unreal, seen by mind, and objects of each other.

In the Kārikā 2.32: no dissolution, no origination, none bound, no striver, none seeking liberation, none liberated: this is the ultimate. Developed in prakaraṇas 3 and 4. | In the Kārikā ch.3: nothing is born in truth; birth is by māyā alone; the immortal does not become mortal; no jīva is born; this is the highest truth (3.2, 3.19–3.28, 3.48). | In prakaraṇa 4: disputants who hold birth of the existent or non-existent proclaim non-birth (4.3–4.5); nothing is born from itself, another, both or neither (4.22); dharmas are unborn and by nature free of old age and death (4.10, 4.29); no jīva is born (4.71); all dharmas are unborn, peaceful, equal (4.91–4.93).
In the Kārikā 3.3–3.9: the self is like space and the jīvas like pot-spaces; they merge when pots dissolve, are not all soiled by one's dust, and are neither modification nor part of the self.
In the Kārikā 3.31–3.32: when the mind becomes no-mind, or by awakening to the truth of the self no longer conceives, duality is not perceived.

name: Restraint of the mind and its faults (Kārikā 3.40–3.46)

definitions.definition: The Kārikā makes fearlessness, ending of sorrow, awakening and imperishable peace depend on restraining the mind (3.40); it counsels patience (3.41), and treats distraction (vikṣepa), laya, residue (kaṣāya) and relishing of the happiness (āsvāda, named rasāsvāda by commentators) with a counsel for each (3.42–3.45); when the mind is neither absorbed nor distracted it is brahman (3.46).

In the Kārikā 3.39 and 4.2: the "contactless" yoga, hard for all yogins to see and feared by them; at 4.2 it is called happy and beneficial for all beings, free of dispute and contradiction. | At 4.2 the "contactless" yoga is saluted as bringing happiness to all beings, beneficial, free of dispute and contradiction; at 3.39 it is hard to see and feared by yogins.

name: The five sheaths (pañcakośa) as referred to in the Kārikā

definitions.definition: In the Kārikā 3.11: the sheaths of the Taittirīya, beginning with rasa, whose self is the supreme jīva shown like space.

name: The critique of cause and effect (Kārikā 4.11–4.23)

definitions.definition: In 4.11–4.23: arguments against birth by cause and effect — if effect is cause, the cause is born; sequence, simultaneity and mutual dependence fail; seed and sprout is as unproven as what it proves; conclusion: nothing born from itself or another, whether existent, non-existent or both.

In 4.47–4.52: as a moving firebrand appears straight or crooked and, still, is without appearance, so consciousness in vibration appears as grasped and grasper and, not vibrating, is without appearance and unborn; the appearances come from nowhere and enter nowhere.

The Kārikā lists four positions on birth (self, other; existent, non-existent, both) and denies them (4.22), and four positions on existence and on motion by which the childish cover the Lord (4.83–4.84).

name: Vocabulary of designation, sign, dependence and awakening in Kārikā ch.4

definitions.definition: Terms used in prakaraṇa 4 and recorded as the text uses them: prajñapti, nimitta, paratantra, saṃkleśa (4.24–4.25), vijñāna and ābhāsa (4.45–4.52), lakṣaṇa-śūnya (4.67), kalpita and saṃvṛti (4.73–4.74), ādibuddha, kṣānti, sunirvṛta, viśārada (4.92–4.93), buddha, tāyin, nāyaka, agrayāna (4.90, 4.98–4.99). No verdict is given on the sources or affinities of this vocabulary.

name: Convention (saṃvṛti) and the ultimate (paramārtha) in the Kārikā

definitions.definition: In 4.57: by convention everything is born (so nothing eternal); in true being all is unborn (so no annihilation). In 4.73–4.74: what exists by imagined or dependent convention does not exist ultimately. At 2.32 and 3.18 the ultimate is stated; 4.42 says birth was taught to those afraid of non-birth.
The Kārikā says accounts of creation (clay, iron, sparks) are a means (3.15) and that birth was taught by the awakened to those always afraid of non-birth (4.42).

name: Worldly and beyond-worldly duality; threefold knowledge (Kārikā 4.87–4.89)

definitions.definition: In 4.87–4.88: duality with an object and apprehension is worldly; without an object but with apprehension is "purely worldly"; without object and apprehension is beyond the world. Knowledge, knowable and to-be-known are proclaimed; knowing them in order gives omniscience (4.89).
